source_text: Ut igitur in Domino nubas secundum Legem et Apostolum (si tamen vel hoc curas), qualis est id matrimonium postulans, quod eis a quibus postulas, non licet habere; ab episcopo monogamo, a presbyteris et diaconis ejusdem sacramenti, a viduis, quarum sectam in te recusasti? Et illi plane sic dabunt viros et uxores, quomodo buccellas. Hoc enim est apud illos: Omni petenti te dabis. Et conjungent vos in Ecclesia virgine, unius Christi unica sponsa. Et orabis pro maritis tuis, novo et vetere. Elige cui te adulteram praestes. Puto, ambobus. Quod si sapias, taceas defuncto. Repudium sit illi silentium tuum, alienis jam dotalibus scriptum. Hoc modo novum promereberis maritum, si veteris obliviscaris. Debes magis illi placere, propter quem Deo placere non maluisti. Haec Psychici volunt Apostolum probasse, aut in totum non recogitasse, cum scriberet: Mulier vincta est in quantum temporis vivit vir ejus; si autem mortuus fuerit, libera est: cui vult, nubat; tantum in Domino. Ex hoc enim capitulo defendunt licentiam secundi matrimonii, imo et plurimi, si secundi; quod enim semel esse desiit, omni obnoxium est numero. Quo autem sensu Apostolus scripserit, ita relucebit, si prius constet, non hoc illum sensu scripsisse, quo Psychici utuntur. Constabit autem, si quis ea recordetur, quae huic capitulo diversa sunt et apud doctrinam, et apud voluntatem, et apud propriam ipsius Pauli disciplinam. Si enim secundas nuptias permittit, quae ab initio non fuerunt, quomodo adfirmat omia ab initium recolligi in Christo? Si vult nos iterare conjugia, quomodo semen nostrum in Isaac semel marito auctore defendit? Quomodo totum ordinem Ecclesiae de monogamis disponit, si non haec disciplina praecedit in laicis, ex quibus Ecclesiae ordo proficit? Quomodo in matrimonio adhuc positos a fructu matrimonii avocat, dicens in collecto esse tempus, si per mortem matrimonio elapsos iterum in matrimonium revocat? Haec si diversa sunt ei capitulo, de quo agitur, constabit, ut diximus, non hoc illum sensu scripsisse, quo Psychici utuntur. Quia facilius est, ut aliquam rationem habeat unum illud capitulum, quae cum caeteris sapiat, quam ut Apostolus diversa inter se docuisse videatur. Eam rationem in ipsa materia poterimus recognoscere. Quae ista materia Apostolo fuit scribendi talia? Tyrocinium novae et cum maxime orientis Ecclesiae, quam lacte scilicet educabat, nondum solido cibo validioris doctrinae: adeo ut, prae illa infantia fidei, ignorarent adhuc quid sibi agendum esset circa carnis et sexus necessitatem. Cujus etiam ipsas species ex rescriptis intelligimus, cum dicit: De his autem quae scribitis, bonum est homini mulierem non attingere; propter fornicationes autem, unusquisque uxorem suam habeat: ostendit fuisse qui in matrimonio a fide deprehensi, verebantur ne non liceret eis matrimonio suo exinde uti, quia in carnem sanctam Christi credidissent. Et tamen secundum veniam concedit, non secundum imperium; id est, indulgens, non praecipiens ita fieri. Caeterum, malebat omnes id esse quod et ipse. Proinde et de repudio rescribens, demonstrat quosdam de isto quoque cogitasse: vel maxime, quia et in ethnicis matrimoniis non putabant post fidem sibi perseverandum. Quaerebant et de virginibus consilium (praeceptum enim Domini non erat), bonum esse homini si sic permaneat; utique quomodo a fide fuerit inventus. Vinctus es uxori, ne quaesieris solutionem. Solutus es ab uxore, non quaesieris uxorem: si autem acceperis uxorem non deliquisti: quia ante fidem soluto ab uxore, non numerabitur post fidem secunda uxor, quae post fidem prima est. A fide enim etiam ipsa vita nostra censetur. Sed hic parcere se dicit illis: alioquin pressuram carnis subsecuturam, prae angustiis temporum impedimenta matrimonii recusantibus; quin potius de Domino sollicitudinem habendam promerendo, quam de marito. Et ita revocat quod permisit. Sic ergo in eodem ipso capitulo, quo definit unumquemque, in qua vocatione vocabitur, in ea permanere debere, adjiciens: Mulier vincta est, quamdiu vivit vir ejus: si autem dormierit, libera est; cui volet nubat, tantum in Domino; hinc quoque eam demonstrat intelligendam, quae et ipsa sic fuerit inventa soluta a viro, quomodo et vir solutus ab uxore; per mortem utique, non per repudium facta solutione: quia repudiatis non permitteret nubere, adversus pristinum praeceptum. Itaque mulier si nupserit, non delinquet, quia nec hic secundus maritus deputabitur, qui est a fide primus, et adeo sic est, ut propterea adjecerit: Tantum in Domino; quia de ea agebatur, quae ethnicum habuerat, et amisso eo crediderat; ne scilicet etiam post fidem ethnico se nubere posse praesumeret; licet nec hoc Psychici curent. Sciamus plane non sic esse in graeco authentico, quomodo in usum exiit per duarum syllabarum aut callidam aut simplicem eversionem: Si dormierit vir ejus, quasi de futuro sonet, ac per hoc videatur ad eam pertinere, quae jam in fide virum amiserit. Hoc quidem si ita esset, in infinitum emissa licentia, totiens virum dedisset, quotiens amissus esset, sine ullo pudore nubendi, etiam ethnicis congruente. Sed etsi ita esset quasi de futuro: Si cujus maritus mortuus fuerit, tantumdem et futurum ad eam pertineret, cujus ante fidem morietur maritus Quaevis accipe, dum caetera non evertas. Nam cum et illa sententiae cedant, servus vocatus es, ne curaveris: Impraeputiatus vocatus es, ne circumcidaris: Circumcisus vocatus es, ne adduxeris; quibus concurrit: Vinctus es uxori, ne quaesieris solutionem: solutus es ab uxore, ne quaesieris uxorem; satis manifestum est, ad eos haec pertinere, qui in nova et recenti vocatione constituti, de his consulebant, in quibus a fide fuerant deprehensi. Haec erit interpretatio capituli istius de hoc examinanda, an et tempori, et caussae, et tam exemplis et argumentis praecedentibus, quam et sententiis et sensibus subsequentibus; et in primis, an ipsius Apostoli et consilio proprio congruat et instituto: nihil enim custodiendum est, quam ne diversus sibi quis deprehendatur.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, so that you may marry in the Lord according to the Law and the Apostle (if indeed you care about this), what kind of marriage is it that you are seeking, which is not permitted for those from whom you are seeking it: from a monogamous bishop, from presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament, from widows, whose sect you have rejected in yourself? And they will plainly give husbands and wives in the same way as they give morsels. For this is their principle: to everyone who asks, you will give. And they will join you in the Church, a virgin, the unique bride of the one Christ. And you will pray for your husbands, new and old. Choose to whom you will offer yourself as an adulteress. I think, to both. But if you are wise, you will be silent about the deceased. Let your silence be a repudiation to him, already written in the dowry documents of others. In this way, you will bring forth a new husband, if you forget the old one. You ought to please him more, for whom you did not wish to please God. The Psychics want to prove that the Apostle approved this, or did not consider it at all, when he wrote: A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives; if her husband dies, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. From this chapter, they defend the license of a second marriage, or even many, if it is a second; for what has once ceased to be is subject to every number. But in what sense the Apostle wrote this will become clear, if it is first established that he did not write it in the sense in which the Psychics use it. It will be established, if someone recalls the things that are different from this chapter, both in doctrine and in will and in the proper discipline of Paul himself. For if he permits second marriages, which were not from the beginning, how does he affirm that all things are gathered together in Christ from the beginning? If he wants us to repeat marriages, how does he defend our seed in Isaac, with one husband as author? How does he arrange the entire order of the Church from monogamists, if this discipline does not precede among the laity, from whom the order of the Church profits? How does he call away those still in marriage from the fruit of marriage, saying that the time is at hand, if through death he calls them back into marriage after they have lapsed from marriage? If these things are different from the chapter in question, it will be established, as we have said, that he did not write it in the sense in which the Psychics use it. Because it is easier for that one chapter to have some reason that agrees with the others, than for the Apostle to seem to have taught diverse things. We will be able to recognize this reason in the subject matter itself. What was the subject matter for the Apostle to write such things? The training of the new and especially the rising Church, which he was nourishing with milk, not yet with solid food of stronger doctrine: so much so that, because of that infancy of faith, they still did not know what they should do regarding the necessity of the flesh and sex. We understand even the species of these things from his writings, when he says: Now concerning the things you wrote, it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornications, let each man have his own wife: he shows that there were those who, having been caught in marriage by faith, were afraid that it was not permitted for them to use their marriage from then on, because they had believed in the holy flesh of Christ. And yet he concedes this according to permission, not according to command; that is, indulging, not prescribing it to be done thus. Moreover, he preferred that all be what he himself was. Therefore, also writing back concerning repudiation, he shows that some were thinking about this as well: especially because they did not think they should persevere in ethnic marriages after faith. They were seeking counsel about virgins (for the command of the Lord was not), that it is good for a man to remain thus; certainly, just as he was found by faith. You are bound to your wife, do not seek a divorce. You are free from your wife, do not seek a wife: but if you do receive a wife, you do not sin: because, having been free from your wife before faith, a second wife after faith will not be counted, which is the first after faith. For from faith, even our life itself is judged. But here he says that he is sparing them: otherwise, the pressure of the flesh would follow, and those who refuse the impediments of marriage because of the difficulties of the times would be hindered; rather, one should have solicitude for the Lord, earning it, than for a husband. And thus he revokes what he permitted. So therefore, in the same chapter in which he defines that each one ought to remain in the calling in which he was called, adding: A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives: if her husband dies, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord; from this, he also demonstrates that she is to be understood, who has been found free from her husband, just as a man is free from his wife; certainly through death, not through repudiation, the divorce having been made: because he would not permit those who have been repudiated to marry, against the former command. Therefore, if a woman marries, she does not sin, because neither will a second husband be assigned to her, who is the first after faith, and thus it is, so that he added: Only in the Lord; because he was dealing with her who had an ethnic husband and, having lost him, believed; lest, indeed, she also presume that she can marry an ethnic man after faith; although the Psychics do not care about this. Let us know plainly that it is not so in the authentic Greek, as it has come into use through the clever or simple reversal of two syllables: If her husband dies, as if it sounds like the future, and thus seems to pertain to her who has already lost her husband in faith. For if it were so, the license would be given infinitely, as many times as the husband has been lost, without any shame in marrying, even to ethnic men. But even if it were so, as if about the future: If a woman's husband has died, it would pertain to her in the same way, whose husband will die before faith. Take whatever you will, as long as you do not overturn the rest. For when even those sentences yield, a slave you were called, do not be concerned: uncircumcised you were called, do not be circumcised: circumcised you were called, do not become uncircumcised; to which is added: You are bound to your wife, do not seek a divorce: you are free from your wife, do not seek a wife; it is sufficiently clear that these pertain to those who, having been established in a new and recent calling, were seeking counsel about those things in which they had been caught by faith. This will be the interpretation of that chapter, to be examined regarding whether it pertains to the time, and the cause, and both the preceding examples and arguments, and the subsequent sentences and meanings; and first, whether it agrees with the counsel and institution of the Apostle himself: for nothing is to be guarded against, lest someone be found to be diverse from himself.

choices.why: referring to remarriage after death or divorce

pass_b_english: If you really want to marry "in the Lord" according to the Law and the Apostle, what kind of marriage are you after, when the very people you petition—a monogamous bishop, presbyters and deacons of the same sacrament, widows whose sect you rejected in yourself—are forbidden to have it? They will hand out husbands and wives as casually as morsels of bread, for their rule is: "Give to everyone who asks you" (Luke 6:30). They will join you in the Church, that virgin, the unique bride of the one Christ, and then you will pray for your husbands—new and old alike. Choose which one you will offer yourself to as an adulteress; I suspect it will be both. But if you have any sense, you will keep silent about the deceased one. Let your silence serve as your repudiation of him, already inscribed in another woman's marriage contract. That is how you will produce a new husband: by forgetting the old. You ought to please this new man more, since you chose not to please God for his sake. (1 Corinthians 7:39)

The Psychics want to prove that the Apostle approved this arrangement—or simply never considered it—when he wrote: "A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, only in the Lord." From this passage they defend the license for a second marriage, indeed for as many as you like once you allow a second; for what has ceased to be once is subject to every number. But the sense in which the Apostle wrote will become clear only if we first establish that he did not write it in the sense the Psychics exploit. That will be established if anyone recalls the things that clash with this chapter—in doctrine, in will, and in Paul's own proper discipline. If he permits second marriages, which did not exist from the beginning, how can he affirm that all things are gathered up again in Christ from the beginning (Ephesians 1:10)? If he wants us to repeat marriages, how does he defend our lineage in Isaac, authored by one husband? How does he constitute the entire order of the Church from monogamists, if that discipline does not precede among the laity, from whom the Church's order arises? How does he call those still in marriage away from its fruit, saying "the appointed time has grown short" (1 Corinthians 7:29), if through death he recalls them back into marriage after they have lapsed from it? If these things contradict the chapter in question, it will stand proved, as we said, that he did not write it in the sense the Psychics use. For it is easier for that one chapter to have some rationale that harmonizes with the others than for the Apostle to appear to teach contradictory things. We can discern that rationale in the subject matter itself. (1 Corinthians 7:39)

What was the occasion for the Apostle to write such things? It was the training of the new and especially the rising Church, which he was still feeding with milk, not yet with the solid food of stronger doctrine—so much so that, in that infancy of faith, they did not yet know what to do about the necessity of flesh and sex. We can see the very shape of these issues from his replies. When he says: "Now concerning the matters about which you wrote: It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman. But because of the temptation to sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife" (1 Corinthians 7:1-2), he shows there were those who, caught in marriage by faith, feared it was no longer permitted for them to use their marriage, because they had believed in the holy flesh of Christ. Yet he concedes this by permission, not by command—that is, indulging them, not prescribing it. Moreover, he preferred that all be as he himself was. So also, writing back concerning divorce, he shows that some were thinking along those lines as well—especially because they did not think they should persevere in pagan marriages after faith. They sought counsel about virgins (for there was no command of the Lord), that it is good for a man to remain as he is; certainly, just as he was found by faith. "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned" (1 Corinthians 7:27-28): because, having been freed from a wife before faith, a second wife after faith will not be counted as a second, since she is the first after faith. For from faith onward, even our life itself is reckoned. But here he says he is sparing them: otherwise the pressure of the flesh would follow, and those who refuse the burdens of marriage because of the distress of the present time would be hindered—rather, one should have solicitude for the Lord, to secure it, than for a husband. And thus he revokes what he permitted. (1 Corinthians 7:25-28)

So then, in the very chapter where he defines that each one ought to remain in the calling in which he was called, adding: "A woman is bound as long as her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is free; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord"—from this he also demonstrates that the woman to be understood here is one who has been found free from her husband just as a man is free from his wife: certainly through death, not through repudiation, the divorce having been made; because he would not permit the divorced to marry, against the former command. Therefore, if a woman marries, she does not sin, because neither will a second husband be reckoned to her, who is the first after faith; and it is so precisely that he added: "Only in the Lord"—because he was dealing with a woman who had a pagan husband and, having lost him, believed; lest she also presume that she can marry a pagan after faith—though the Psychics do not care about this. Let us know plainly that the authentic Greek does not read as it has come into use through the clever or simple reversal of two syllables: "If her husband dies," as if it sounds like the future, and thus seems to pertain to her who has already lost her husband in the faith. For if it were so, the license would extend infinitely—as many times as a husband is lost, she could marry without any shame, even to pagans. But even if it were so, as if about the future: "If a woman's husband has died," it would pertain equally to her whose husband will die before faith. Take whatever reading you will, as long as you do not overturn the rest. For when even those sentences yield—"Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it. Were you called uncircumcised? Do not become circumcised. Were you called circumcised? Do not become uncircumcised" (1 Corinthians 7:21, 18)—to which is added: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife" (1 Corinthians 7:27)—it is sufficiently clear that these pertain to those who, established in a new and recent calling, were seeking counsel about the very things in which they had been caught by faith. This will be the interpretation of that chapter to be examined—whether it fits the time, the cause, both the preceding examples and arguments, and the subsequent sentences and senses; and first, whether it agrees with the Apostle's own counsel and institution: for nothing is more to be guarded against than that someone be found to be at odds with himself. (1 Corinthians 7:39, 1 Corinthians 7:25-28)
notes: The text is a discussion on marriage and remarriage in the context of Christian faith and doctrine.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments of Tertullian regarding the interpretation of 1 Corinthians 7. All scripture citations in Pass B (Luke 6:30, Ephesians 1:10, 1 Corinthians 7:1-2, 7:27-28, 7:25-28, 7:21, 7:18, 7:39) are correctly mapped to the Latin text's allusions or direct quotes. The distinction between 'permission' (veniam) and 'command' (imperium) is preserved. The technical discussion regarding the Greek syllable reversal is handled faithfully.
